content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: For unique indexes, begin with evidence from representative queries and data. Read the execution plan and compare measured behavior before changing indexes or query structure; keep both correctness and write costs in view.

items.title: Enforcing uniqueness
items.text: Enforcing uniqueness helps you understand query access paths and use indexes selectively, weighing measured read improvements against storage and write costs. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Unique indexes vs. unique constraints
items.text: Unique indexes vs. unique constraints should be expressed as a database rule where practical, not only as an application convention. Test duplicate values and missing references so that invalid states are rejected consistently.

items.title: Indexing composite values
items.text: Indexing composite values should be evaluated with measurements on representative data. Inspect the plan, estimated versus actual row counts where available, and the workload's read/write balance; an index or rewrite is not automatically faster.

items.title: NULL semantics across engines
items.text: NULL semantics across engines requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
